big_idea: Executive presence, not merit alone, is what gets people promoted into senior leadership, and it rests on three measurable pillars: gravitas, communication, and appearance.

tool.label: The Three Pillars Framework (Gravitas / Communication / Appearance)
tool.text: Hewlett's research-based model breaks executive presence into three weighted components: gravitas, roughly two-thirds of the perception, covering confidence, decisiveness, integrity, and grace under fire; communication, about a quarter, covering speaking skill, voice, and the ability to read a room; and appearance, a small remainder, polished, appropriate self-presentation. Leaders can audit and deliberately strengthen each pillar rather than treating presence as an innate trait.
tool.note: The percentage weightings come from Hewlett's own executive surveys and shift slightly between the original book and the Executive Presence 2.0 edition.

ideas.title: Gravitas is the entry ticket
ideas.text: Composure under pressure, decisiveness, and integrity in high-stakes moments determine whether others trust a leader's judgment.

ideas.title: Communication carries the message
ideas.text: Voice, storytelling, eye contact, and reading the room determine whether gravitas even gets noticed.

ideas.title: Appearance is a threshold, not a ceiling
ideas.text: Looking the part removes a distraction, but polish can't substitute for substance.

ideas.title: Double binds for women
ideas.text: Assertiveness often reads as abrasive while accommodation reads as weak, narrowing the acceptable behavioral band.

ideas.title: Sponsors over mentors
ideas.text: Advancement depends less on private advice and more on advocates who speak up for you when you're not in the room.

ideas.title: Presence is learnable
ideas.text: Case examples show presence can be deliberately built through practice, not just inherited.

try_it: Record yourself giving a 2-minute update, count filler words and rushed sentences, then re-record it cleaner.
Ask a trusted colleague for one specific piece of presence feedback this week and visibly act on it.
Before your next high-stakes meeting, write and rehearse a one-sentence point of view so you can state it without notes.
Identify one senior person who could sponsor, not just mentor, you and ask for a specific, visible opportunity.
best_for: Mid-career professionals preparing for a promotion into senior leadership
Women and underrepresented professionals navigating bias in how presence is judged
less_useful: Early-career individual contributors with little exposure to senior rooms yet
Readers wanting a psychological deep-dive rather than a practitioner framework built on survey data

related.why: A different author's take on the same topic, focused more on personal branding and perception
A shorter HBR collection on the closely related skill of leadership presence
